request: This is a legacy C++ JavaScript interpreter with no product docs. Tell me what it does, who it is for, and how we would rebuild it in Rust with the same behaviour.
summary: tiny-js is a small embeddable JavaScript interpreter in C++: a host application creates a CTinyJS, registers native C++ functions, and executes or evaluates script text directly from source. It ships a command-line runner that executes script files or a line-by-line interactive mode, and a test runner over 38 numbered scripts. Who embeds it today is not in the code.

engineering.claim: The interpreter is one class, CTinyJS, whose public API is execute, evaluateComplex, evaluate, addNative, getScriptVariable, getVariable, setVariable, and trace, with the symbol table exposed as root.

Script text is executed directly by a recursive-descent parser with one method per precedence level (functionCall, factor, unary, term, expression, shift, condition, logic, ternary, base, block, statement); there is no intermediate code.
Values are CScriptVar nodes whose children are a linked list of CScriptVarLink, so object member and array index lookup walk the list.
Memory is managed by reference counting (ref and unref), so a cycle such as a.foo = a is never freed.

The command-line runner executes each file argument in one interpreter in order and exits 0; with no arguments it prints a banner and executes stdin line by line (lines up to 2047 bytes) until quit() is called.
A script error in file mode prints 'ERROR: ' followed by the message and the position, and the runner exits 1; in interactive mode it prints the error and continues.

The command-line runner registers the general built-ins and console.log, print, and dump, but not the Math functions; the test runner registers both sets, so Math.abs and the rest exist in tests but not in the command-line runner.
Script can run arbitrary script text at run time through the built-ins exec and eval, which call execute and evaluateComplex on the same interpreter.

Make builds run_tests and Script, and CMake builds a static library tiny-js plus tiny-js-cli and tiny-js-tests, all from TinyJS.cpp, TinyJS_Functions.cpp, and TinyJS_MathFunctions.cpp; CMake requires C++14 outside Windows.
The interpreter uses only the C and C++ standard libraries; glibc's mcheck, execinfo, and malloc hooks appear only in the test runner behind MTRACE and INSANE_MEMORY_DEBUG.

run_tests runs tests/test001.js upwards until the first missing number, and a test passes when the script leaves the global result truthy; on failure it writes the symbol table as JSON to <file>.fail.js. The *.42.js files and tests/42tests are not run by it.
The comment's known-issue list is partly stale: it says the postfix increment returns the current value, but the version history says 0.31 fixed it and the code returns the previous value.
Known language gaps: Array(5) does not create an array of that length, length cannot be set, and there is no prefix increment operator.
run_test formats '<filename>.fail.js' into a 64-byte stack buffer with sprintf, so a test path longer than 55 characters overflows it.

Errors are thrown as heap pointers (throw new CScriptException) and execute rethrows a new one, so every caught script error leaks its exception object unless the host deletes it; Script.cpp never does.
Math.rand and Math.randInt call rand() and nothing seeds it, so a given build repeats the same sequence on every run; the sequence depends on the C library.
engineering.reasoning: No srand call appears in the indexed sources (the index records rand as the only random surface), and the C standard defines an unseeded rand as seeded with 1.

engineering.claim: Open TODOs in the source: a va-args helper to call a script function from C++, eval of statements as well as expressions, moving shift into mathsOp, a call whose purpose the author questions, and a better way to parse the left-hand side of a for-in.

capabilities.name: Run JavaScript-like scripts
capabilities.claim: Executes script text with variables, functions, objects with prototype inheritance, arrays, the ternary, shift, and modulo operators, from source.

capabilities.name: Evaluate an expression for the host
capabilities.claim: Returns the value of script text to C++ as a string (evaluate) or a value link (evaluateComplex).

capabilities.name: Call C++ from script
capabilities.claim: A host registers a native C++ function under a script name and signature, including methods on built-in classes such as String.substring.

capabilities.name: Read and set script variables from C++
capabilities.claim: The host reads or sets a variable by dotted path, or prints every variable to stdout (trace).

capabilities.name: JSON in and out
capabilities.claim: Serialises any value to JSON (JSON.stringify, getJSON) and reads JSON back by evaluating it as script.

capabilities.name: Built-in library
capabilities.claim: Provides string, array, integer, object, and JSON built-ins, exec and eval, and a Math library of 29 functions when registered.

capabilities.name: Command-line and interactive runner
capabilities.claim: Runs script files from the command line or reads statements interactively, printing with print and console.log and dumping the symbol table with dump.

capabilities.name: Work with script values from C++
capabilities.claim: The public header exposes the script value type to the host: typed get, set, and type tests (getInt, setString, isArray), children and array elements by name or index, reference counting (ref, unref), a native callback per function value, and the links that name a value (CScriptVarLink).

capabilities.name: Tokenise script text and quote strings
capabilities.claim: The public header also exposes the lexer (CScriptLex: match a token, take a sub-lexer, report a position as line and column), the exception scripts' errors are thrown as (CScriptException, with its text), and getJSString, which quotes a C++ string for script.

capabilities.name: Run the bundled test scripts
capabilities.claim: run_tests runs the one script named on its command line, or each tests/testNNN.js from 001 until a number is missing, with the built-in and Math functions registered; a script passes when it leaves result true, and a failing script's symbols are written to <file>.fail.js.

product_claims.claim: The README addresses developers of applications that need a simple, familiar scripting language with no dependencies beyond the normal C++ libraries.
The README names two jobs: scripting simple behaviour, and loading and saving settings.
It is not meant to be fast, full-featured, or standards-compliant, and slow loops are accepted.
Which applications embed tiny-js today, and which of its APIs they call, is not in the repository.
product_claims.question: Q1

product_claims.claim: Whether the Rust version must keep today's quirks (the non-standard behaviour in E12 and E13) or may correct them is not in the code.
product_claims.question: Q2

product_claims.claim: Whether hosts load scripts they do not control, which decides how much exec and eval (E8) must be sandboxed, is not in the code.
product_claims.question: Q3

product_claims.claim: The README points to a more complete fork (42tiny-js) and a microcontroller rewrite (Espruino), so the product sits among alternatives.

questions.question: Which applications embed tiny-js today, and do they call it through the C++ classes (CTinyJS, CScriptVar) or only through execute, evaluate, and addNative?
questions.why: It decides whether the Rust version needs a C ABI for existing hosts, and which API the parity cases must cover.
questions.default: Keep a C ABI for execute, evaluate, addNative, getVariable, and setVariable only, because the README sells calling C/C++ from script (P1) and those are the documented entry points.

questions.question: Must the Rust version reproduce today's behaviour exactly, including the known gaps (Array(5), length not settable, no prefix ++), or may it correct them?
questions.why: It decides whether the golden outputs are the contract or a starting point, and which case sets exclude behaviour.
questions.default: Reproduce exactly in the first release so existing scripts keep working; correct each gap later as its own Story with a new golden case.

questions.question: Do any hosts run scripts from users or files they do not control?
questions.why: If they do, exec and eval and unbounded loops need limits (time, memory) in the Rust version, which changes its design.
questions.default: Assume scripts are trusted (settings and simple behaviour, P2) and record a limit on execution time as a later Story.

questions.question: Is the command-line runner part of the product, or a demo of embedding?
questions.why: If it is a product, its output format and its missing Math functions (E7) become part of the contract.
questions.default: A demo: keep it for parity tests, register the same built-ins as the test runner only if the answer says so.

questions.question: Is reproducing the same Math.rand sequence required?
questions.why: An unseeded C rand() sequence (E16) cannot be reproduced portably in Rust.
questions.default: No: exclude random output from parity and test only the range.

modernisation.strategy: Characterise first, then port behind the same interfaces: capture golden outputs from the C++ build for the 38 test scripts and the command-line runner, port the lexer and values, then the parser and built-ins, and keep a C ABI shim so existing hosts can switch without code changes (pending Q1). Retire the C++ build only when every case set matches.

steps.title: Capture golden outputs from the C++ build
Port the lexer and the value model (reference counting replaced by Rc and a cycle collector or arena)
Port the built-in and Math libraries
Expose the embedding API as a Rust crate and a C ABI, then retire the C++ build

risks.claim: Error messages include the parser's line and column, so a Rust parser must report positions exactly as the C++ lexer does for G3 to pass.
Doubles are converted to text with C's %f format (six decimals: 50 prints as 50.000000), which Rust's default formatting does not match.

compatibility.name: Embedding API: CTinyJS execute, evaluate, evaluateComplex, addNative, and the CScriptVar classes
compatibility.consumers: applications that embed the interpreter (unknown; Q1 asks)

compatibility.name: Script output and ERROR lines printed by the command-line runner
Runner exit code: 0 after the scripts run, 1 on a script error
Command-line runner: script paths as arguments, interactive mode without them
compatibility.consumers: unknown; Q4 asks whether the runner is part of the product
